commands.name: chmod
commands.risk_reason: Incorrect permissions can expose files or break applications.
cautions: Avoid `chmod -R 777` — it makes everything world-writable and is almost never the real fix.
Recursive changes treat files and directories alike; use capital X or `find -type d`/`-type f` separately.
Find the real cause of “permission denied” with `namei -l <path>`.
commands.explanation: chmod modifies read/write/execute permissions for owner, group, and others. Accepts symbolic (u+x) or octal (755) notation. Octal is precise and unambiguous — 755 means owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x. The -R flag applies changes recursively.

flags.desc: Print a message for each changed file
Report only files that are changed

examples.desc: Restrict private key to owner-read only (SSH requirement)
Readable by all, writable only by owner
Set app directory: owner rwx, group r-x, others none
Set SUID bit — runs as file owner

safer.why: Capital X sets execute only on directories and already-executable files.

commands.pro_tip: Remember '7=rwx, 6=rw-, 5=r-x, 4=r--'. Use 644 for files, 755 for directories as baseline public defaults — and 600/700 for anything private.

commands.name: chown
commands.summary: Change file or directory ownership (user and/or group).
commands.risk_reason: Changing ownership of system files can break services.
cautions: Recursive chown on system directories breaks services that rely on their own UID.
-R does not follow symlinks by default; -L follows them and can reach outside the tree.
Record ownership first: getfacl -R <path> > acl.backup.
commands.explanation: chown changes the owner and/or group of files. Format is user:group. Either can be omitted — chown user: changes owner and group to user's primary group; chown :group changes only the group.

flags.desc: Print a message for each changed file

examples.desc: Set web root to nginx user and group
Recursively set ownership for app directory

safer.why: Change only files owned by a specific user.

commands.pro_tip: Use `chown user:` (trailing colon, no group) to change the user and automatically set group to that user's primary group — saves a lookup step.

commands.name: useradd
commands.summary: Create a new user account on the Linux system.
commands.risk_reason: Creates system access; poor configuration can introduce security vulnerabilities.
cautions: Without -m no home directory is created; without -s the login shell may default to /bin/sh.
Adding users to sudo/wheel/docker groups grants root-equivalent access.
For service accounts use -r and -s /usr/sbin/nologin.
commands.explanation: useradd creates user accounts in /etc/passwd. -m creates a home directory, -s sets the login shell, -G adds to supplementary groups, -r creates a service account without login. On Debian/Ubuntu, `adduser` is the friendlier interactive wrapper.

flags.desc: Create a home directory for the new user
Create a system account (no home, no interactive login)

examples.desc: Create deploy user with home, bash, and sudo+docker access
Create a service account with no login shell for Prometheus
Create alice with a specific UID and developers group

commands.pro_tip: For service accounts always use `-r -s /usr/sbin/nologin` — prevents interactive login while still allowing the service to run as that user.

commands.name: passwd
commands.summary: Change or set a user account password.
commands.risk_reason: Locking or changing passwords affects user access.
cautions: `passwd -l` on the only admin or root account can lock everybody out.
`passwd -d` removes the password (an empty password).
Prefer SSH keys and enforce policy with chage.
commands.explanation: passwd updates /etc/shadow. Root can change any user's password. -l locks an account, -u unlocks, -e forces a password change on next login.

flags.desc: Force password change on next login

examples.desc: Force deploy user to set a new password on next login
Lock tempuser account during an investigation

commands.pro_tip: Use `chage -l username` to view password expiry info including last changed date and warning period.

commands.name: openssl
commands.summary: Cryptography toolkit — TLS testing, key/certificate generation, and data encoding.
commands.risk_reason: Weak key sizes or mishandled private keys create serious security vulnerabilities.
cautions: Never share private keys; protect them with chmod 600 and a passphrase.
Use RSA ≥ 3072 or ECDSA/Ed25519 and SHA-256+; avoid SHA-1/MD5.
-nodes / -noenc writes the private key unencrypted.
commands.explanation: openssl is a comprehensive crypto toolkit. It generates RSA/EC keys, creates CSRs, signs certificates, tests TLS handshakes, encodes/decodes base64, and computes hashes. Essential for PKI management, HTTPS setup, and debugging TLS certificate issues.

examples.desc: Test a TLS connection and inspect the full certificate chain for a remote host
Generate a 4096-bit RSA private key and certificate signing request in one step
Check expiry dates of a certificate from a PEM file

commands.pro_tip: Check remote cert expiry without downloading a file: `echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates`

commands.name: ssh-keygen
commands.summary: Generate, inspect, and manage SSH public/private key pairs.
commands.risk_reason: Private keys must be protected — exposure grants unauthorized SSH access.
cautions: Do not overwrite an existing key — check the target path first.
Protect private keys with a passphrase and chmod 600; `ssh-keygen -R` only edits known_hosts.
commands.explanation: ssh-keygen creates key pairs for passwordless SSH authentication. Ed25519 is the modern standard — shorter, faster, and more secure than RSA. -C adds an identifying comment. -f sets the filename. -R removes stale entries from known_hosts.

flags.desc: Key bits — for RSA: minimum 2048, prefer 4096
Comment to identify the key (typically email or hostname)
Output filename for the key pair
Passphrase for the private key ('' for none)
Change the passphrase of an existing private key
Show fingerprint of a public key file

examples.desc: Generate a named Ed25519 key pair for production deployment
Generate a 4096-bit RSA key for legacy system compatibility
Display the fingerprint of a public key for verification

commands.pro_tip: Always prefer Ed25519: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` — the public key is 68 characters vs 800+ for RSA-4096, with stronger security properties.

commands.name: umask
commands.summary: Set default permissions mask for newly created files and directories.
commands.risk_reason: Affects only new files; doesn't change existing ones.
commands.explanation: umask defines which permission bits are removed from new files/directories. The default umask 022 means files are created 644 (666-022) and directories 755 (777-022). A stricter umask 027 gives 640/750 — better for multi-user servers.

examples.desc: New files: owner rw, group r, others none
New files: owner rw only — maximum privacy

commands.pro_tip: Set umask 027 in /etc/profile.d/ for service accounts on production servers — prevents world-readable files from being created accidentally.

commands.name: gpg
commands.summary: GNU Privacy Guard: encrypt, decrypt, sign, and verify files.
commands.risk_reason: Losing private keys permanently locks encrypted data.
cautions: If you lose the private key (or its passphrase) the encrypted data is gone for good — back up keys and the revocation certificate.
`--export-secret-keys` output must stay offline and protected.
Verify fingerprints out-of-band before trusting a key.
commands.explanation: gpg implements the OpenPGP standard for encryption, signing, and key management. Used for encrypting secrets, signing releases and commits, verifying software authenticity, and secure file transfer without shared passwords.

examples.desc: Generate a new GPG key pair

commands.pro_tip: Always back up your private key: `gpg --export-secret-keys --armor user@email.com > private-key.asc`. Store it encrypted offline — key loss = permanent data loss.

commands.name: selinux
commands.summary: Manage SELinux mandatory access control policies.
commands.risk_reason: Setting to permissive/disabled removes security enforcement.
cautions: Setting permissive/disabled removes mandatory access control — fix the denial instead.
chcon changes do not survive a relabel; use semanage fcontext + restorecon.
Going from disabled to enforcing needs a full relabel (touch /.autorelabel) and a reboot.
commands.explanation: SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) enforces mandatory access control policies beyond traditional file permissions. When applications fail silently, SELinux denials are often the cause. Use getenforce/setenforce to check and toggle mode, and audit2why to understand denials.

examples.desc: Set to Permissive (logs denials, doesn't enforce)
Explain recent SELinux denials in plain English

examples.cmd: ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow -M mypolicy && semodule -i mypolicy.pp
examples.desc: Generate and install a policy to fix a denial

safer.why: Find out what is being denied.

commands.pro_tip: Before permanently disabling SELinux, try `setenforce 0` and test — if the issue resolves, use `audit2allow` to create a proper policy instead of leaving enforcement disabled.

commands.name: apparmor
commands.summary: Manage AppArmor mandatory access control profiles.
commands.risk_reason: Disabling profiles removes security enforcement.
cautions: Disabling a profile removes confinement — use aa-complain while debugging instead.
Profile syntax errors can stop services from starting; validate with apparmor_parser -p.
commands.explanation: AppArmor confines processes to defined sets of files, capabilities, and network access using profiles. Default on Ubuntu/Debian. Profiles are stored in /etc/apparmor.d/. aa-status shows which processes are confined, aa-complain sets a profile to log-only mode for debugging.

examples.desc: Show all AppArmor profiles and their modes
Set nginx profile to complain/log mode for debugging
Set nginx profile back to enforce mode
View AppArmor kernel messages and denials

commands.pro_tip: Use `aa-complain` on a problematic profile, reproduce the issue, then check `dmesg | grep apparmor` to see exactly what was denied — build the policy fix from real denials, not guessing.

commands.name: openssl advanced
commands.summary: Advanced OpenSSL: TLS debugging, certificate inspection, and PKI operations.
commands.risk_reason: Generating weak keys or exposing private keys has security implications.
cautions: Self-signed certificates and -k in clients disable trust — use a proper CA for production.
Never paste private keys into tickets or chat tools.
Check expiry before renewals: openssl x509 -noout -enddate.
commands.explanation: Beyond s_client, OpenSSL handles the full certificate lifecycle: inspecting cert details, verifying chains, checking expiry, generating CSRs, and testing specific TLS ciphers and protocol versions. Essential for TLS troubleshooting.

examples.cmd: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

examples.desc: Test specific TLS version and cipher negotiation

commands.pro_tip: Use `openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate` in monitoring scripts to alert on certificate expiry — check daily and alert when < 30 days remain.

commands.name: sudo
commands.summary: Run commands as another user (usually root)
commands.risk_reason: Runs with elevated privileges; one typo can damage the whole system.
cautions: Re-read the whole command before pressing Enter — especially paths and globs.
Avoid `sudo -i`/`sudo su` for routine work; they hide actions from the audit trail.
Never edit /etc/sudoers directly — use visudo.
Redirections run as YOU, not root: `sudo echo x > /etc/f` fails; use `| sudo tee`.
commands.explanation: Executes a command as root or another user according to /etc/sudoers.

flags.caution: May leak your environment into a privileged context.

commands.name: su
commands.risk_reason: Opens a shell with another identity (often root).
cautions: Using su to become root bypasses per-command sudo logging.
Leave the elevated shell as soon as you are done.
commands.explanation: `su -` starts a login shell as the target user.

commands.name: visudo
commands.risk_reason: Mistakes can remove everyone’s sudo access.
cautions: Always keep a second root session open while editing.
NOPASSWD: ALL entries grant unrestricted root without a password — limit to specific commands.
A syntax error can disable sudo entirely if edited with a normal editor.
commands.explanation: Locks and syntax-checks /etc/sudoers before saving.

commands.name: usermod
commands.risk_reason: Changing UID/group/home incorrectly breaks logins and file ownership.
cautions: `usermod -G group user` without -a replaces ALL supplementary groups — you can remove sudo access or lock someone out.
Adding users to sudo, wheel or docker grants root-equivalent access.
Don’t change a logged-in user’s UID/home without planning the migration.
commands.explanation: Edits account attributes: groups, shell, home, login name, lock state.

flags.caution: Without -a the user is REMOVED from all other groups.

commands.name: userdel
commands.risk_reason: Removes the account; with -r also its home directory and mail.
cautions: Back up the home directory first: tar -czf alice-home.tgz /home/alice.
Files owned by the old UID remain and could be re-assigned to a new user with the same UID.
Check running processes and crontabs of the user first.
commands.explanation: Deletes a user from /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.

flags.desc: Remove home directory and mail spool

flags.caution: Even if the user is logged in.

safer.why: Find files owned by the user

commands.name: groupadd
commands.risk_reason: Adds a group; a duplicate GID could cause permission confusion.
commands.explanation: Creates a new group in /etc/group. See the flags and examples below, and run `man groupadd` for the full reference.

commands.name: groupdel
commands.risk_reason: Files owned by the group keep the numeric GID.
cautions: Files with that GID become ownerless and may be reused by a future group.
Cannot delete a user’s primary group.
commands.explanation: Removes a group. See the flags and examples below, and run `man groupdel` for the full reference.

commands.name: chage
commands.risk_reason: Wrong expiry values can lock accounts.
cautions: -E0 expires the account immediately — useful for locking, but easy to do by accident.
Service accounts with max age set can fail unexpectedly.
commands.explanation: Shows or changes password expiry policy per user.

commands.name: ssh-copy-id
commands.summary: Install your public key on a server
commands.risk_reason: Modifies authorized_keys on the remote host.
cautions: Verify the host fingerprint before first login.
Remove old keys when people leave; review authorized_keys regularly.
commands.explanation: Appends your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys remotely.

commands.name: ssh-add
commands.summary: Add keys to the SSH agent
commands.risk_reason: Keeps decrypted keys in memory.
cautions: Forwarding the agent (-A) lets remote root use your keys — prefer ProxyJump.
Use -t to limit key lifetime.
commands.explanation: Loads private keys into ssh-agent. See the flags and examples below, and run `man ssh-add` for the full reference.

examples.desc: Load a key for one hour

commands.name: fail2ban-client
commands.risk_reason: Can unban attackers or ban legitimate IPs; misconfiguration can lock you out.
cautions: Whitelist your own admin IPs (ignoreip) so you cannot ban yourself.
Test jail changes with fail2ban-regex before reloading.
commands.explanation: Queries and manages jails and banned IPs.

commands.name: certbot
commands.summary: Obtain and renew Let’s Encrypt certificates
commands.risk_reason: Can modify web server config and hit rate limits.
cautions: Rate limits: failed validations and force-renewals can block issuance for days.
The nginx/apache plugins edit configuration — back it up.
commands.explanation: ACME client that issues and renews TLS certificates.

commands.name: getenforce
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Prints Enforcing, Permissive or Disabled.

commands.name: setenforce
commands.summary: Switch SELinux between enforcing and permissive
commands.risk_reason: Permissive mode disables enforcement until reboot, weakening protection.
cautions: setenforce 0 is a diagnostic, not a fix — find the denial with ausearch and write policy instead.
Don’t forget to return to enforcing.
commands.explanation: Changes the runtime SELinux mode; does not survive reboot.

commands.name: restorecon
commands.risk_reason: Relabels files, possibly changing which services can access them.
cautions: Run with -n first.
Relabelling / can take very long; scope paths.
commands.explanation: Resets file contexts to policy defaults.

commands.name: semanage
commands.risk_reason: Wrong rules weaken security or break services.
cautions: Changes persist across reboots.
Avoid broad types such as unconfined_t or permissive domains.
commands.explanation: Persistent SELinux configuration: file contexts, ports, booleans, logins.

commands.name: aide
commands.risk_reason: Read-only checking; init overwrites the baseline.
cautions: Store the baseline offline or read-only; an attacker with root can regenerate it.
commands.explanation: Compares the filesystem to a database of hashes to detect tampering.

commands.name: lynis
commands.risk_reason: Read-only system scan.
cautions: Treat suggestions as input, not gospel — test hardening changes on non-production first.
commands.explanation: Runs a hardening audit and prints suggestions.

commands.name: ssh-keyscan
commands.risk_reason: Network probe of hosts.
cautions: Blindly trusting scanned keys defeats host verification — compare fingerprints out-of-band.
commands.explanation: Fetches public host keys for known_hosts.

commands.name: age
commands.risk_reason: Encrypts/decrypts files; losing the key loses the data.
cautions: Back up your key file; there is no recovery.
Delete plaintext originals safely after encrypting.
commands.explanation: Simple file encryption with public keys or passphrases.

commands.name: pass
commands.risk_reason: Stores secrets in GPG files; clipboard exposure.
cautions: Passwords in the clipboard can be read by other apps.
Back up your GPG key.
commands.explanation: Password store backed by gpg and git. See the flags and examples below, and run `man pass` for the full reference.

examples.desc: Copy to the clipboard (cleared after 45 s)

commands.name: adduser
commands.risk_reason: Creates accounts with home directories.
cautions: Set a strong password or SSH key only access.
commands.explanation: Friendly wrapper around useradd. See the flags and examples below, and run `man adduser` for the full reference.

commands.name: deluser
commands.risk_reason: --remove-home deletes files.
cautions: Back up /home/<user> first.
commands.explanation: Debian wrapper for userdel. See the flags and examples below, and run `man deluser` for the full reference.

commands.name: newgrp
commands.risk_reason: Changes group for a subshell.
commands.explanation: Starts a shell with another group. See the flags and examples below, and run `man newgrp` for the full reference.

commands.name: chsh
commands.risk_reason: Wrong shell prevents login.
cautions: Shell must be listed in /etc/shells and installed, otherwise login fails.
commands.explanation: Changes the login shell. See the flags and examples below, and run `man chsh` for the full reference.

commands.name: faillock
commands.risk_reason: Resetting clears protection.
cautions: Resetting hides brute-force attempts — check logs first.
commands.explanation: Manages PAM faillock counters. See the flags and examples below, and run `man faillock` for the full reference.

commands.name: pwck
commands.risk_reason: Check only unless -r omitted.
commands.explanation: Verifies integrity of passwd/shadow. See the flags and examples below, and run `man pwck` for the full reference.

commands.name: openssl x509
commands.risk_reason: Read-only.
commands.explanation: Print dates, subject, fingerprint of certificates.

commands.name: openssl s_client
commands.risk_reason: Network probe.
cautions: -verify_return_error makes failures explicit.
commands.explanation: Connects to a TLS server and shows the chain.

commands.name: openssl req
commands.risk_reason: Private keys must be protected.
cautions: -nodes leaves the key unencrypted — protect with chmod 600.
Self-signed certs are not trusted by clients.
commands.explanation: Generates keys and certificate signing requests.

commands.name: ufw allow
commands.risk_reason: Exposes a service.
cautions: Avoid “allow 22” from anywhere on Internet-facing hosts when a VPN or allow-list is possible.
commands.explanation: Adds an allow rule. See the flags and examples below, and run `man ufw` for the full reference.

examples.cmd: ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 22

safer.cmd: ufw allow from <cidr> to any port <port>
